gov.title: Governance and DevSecOps
gov.banner: A still picture of Chora’s live governance dashboard (O+), taken on {{d}}. This kiosk measures nothing live, so these numbers stay as they were that day.
gov.imda: Singapore’s Model AI Governance Framework (IMDA): its four areas
gov.counts: {{n}} checks: {{p}} met, {{pa}} partly met, {{f}} not yet met
gov.rule: How the colour is set (the same rule the product shows): red if any top-priority check is not met, amber if two or more second-priority checks are not met; third-priority checks never change it. Red is shown honestly: it marks work still to do.
gov.f1: Every Chora service has its own checked release pipeline: it scans the code for security weaknesses, lists every software part inside, signs the result so anyone can check it is the copy that was built, and tests the running service from the outside. The copies on this computer were built here for the showcase, so they are not signed.
gov.f2: In that pipeline, a team of AI agents must pass its own test before release: a score below its pass mark stops the release.
gov.f3: Every AI agent is registered with how much freedom it has: simple low-stakes tasks it may do alone, work a person watches, or work a person must approve. The level beyond these, an AI acting outside the system’s checks and records (Chora’s autonomy level 3), is not allowed: the database will not accept it.
gov.f4: Every decision an AI makes is written to a tamper-evident log, each entry sealed to the one before it, so an auditor can check that none was altered afterwards.
dim.d1w: A record of every decision, where data came from, how long it is kept, and who is responsible for what.
dim.d2w: Explaining how an answer was reached, naming its sources, and tracking which AI model version gave it.
dim.d3w: Safety filters, tests that try to trick the AI, watching that quality does not slip over time, and a backup when a model is unavailable.
dim.d4w: Testing for unfair bias, a person approving important AI decisions, access for people with disabilities, and fair results across different groups of learners.

eng.safety.title: AI safety and evaluation
eng.safety.body: How an AI crew is judged, attacked and stopped before release, and watched after it.
sf.title: AI safety and evaluation
sf.sub: One pipeline, five checks: three before an AI crew is released, two after. Click a stage to see its evidence.
sf.banner: Real results, captured from Chora’s cloud edition on the dates shown (7 to 30 Aug 2026). This computer runs none of these checks, so nothing on this page changes.
sf.pipeAria: The five safety checks, in order
sf.maskNote: Grey boxes hide ids, links and, on 24 Aug, the leaked words.
sf.say.judge: Before release, a judge AI (Google’s Vertex AI Evaluation) scores the crew’s answers to test questions for following instructions and for safety, and every score must reach its pass mark.
sf.rule.judge: To pass, every answer must be judged safe. Following instructions is scored from 1 to 5: the question writer must average at least 3.5, and its critic at least 3.0.
sf.say.redteam: Before release, the crew is attacked six ways, and it must refuse every one: a single attack that gets through is a fail.
sf.rule.redteam: Pass: block rate 1.000, all six attacks refused.
sf.say.gate: On 24 Aug 2026 one of the six attacks got through the question writer, so its block rate was 0.833 against a required 1.000; its critic and its renderer both passed, and the gate still released nothing.
sf.rule.gate: The crew is released as one: if any member misses its bar, or its check fails or runs out of time, nothing ships.
sf.note.gate: Nobody planted this one: the attacks were the same set that had passed before.
sf.say.runtime: After release, in the cloud edition, Cloud Model Armor screens every live AI call on the way in and on the way out; on this computer that screen is simulated and does not run.
sf.rule.runtime: Cloud edition: every call is screened. This computer: not enabled (see “About the app”).
sf.say.drift: After release, the same judge re-scores the live crew on a schedule and compares each score with a stored baseline; a drop of more than 0.5 fails the check and raises an alert, even when the score still clears its pass mark.
sf.rule.drift: The proof below is a planted test: the baseline was set above the top score on purpose, so the check had to refuse.
sf.c.judge-floors.meta: 24 Aug 2026 · Vertex AI Evaluation, in the Cloud Build log
sf.c.judge-floors: The question writer’s two scores, each against its pass mark (the log calls it a “floor”).
sf.c.judge-oplus: The same kind of scores on Chora’s governance console, for the question writer and its critic.
sf.c.redteam-six-blocked: All six attacks refused by the question writer: block rate 1.000.
sf.c.gate-blocked-leak: Five attacks blocked and one leaked (its words are hidden), so GATE BLOCK: 0.833 against 1.000.
sf.c.gate-crew-nothing: The renderer was cleared, yet the crew as a whole promoted nothing.
sf.c.runtime-armor.meta: 30 Aug 2026 · Chora’s AI pipeline trace, cloud edition
sf.c.runtime-armor: Model Armor screening one question job on the way in and on the way out.
sf.c.drift-gate-planted.meta: 18 Aug 2026 · Logs Explorer · a planted test
sf.c.drift-gate-planted: The question writer’s baseline was planted at 5.75, above the top score of 5: it scored 5.000 and was blocked. Its critic, left untouched, passed in the same run.
sf.c.drift-record: The question writer’s scores, run after run (10 to 16 Aug): the record a baseline is taken from.

presenter.title: Presenter
presenter.visitsToday: Demo sessions today (anonymous, on this computer)
talk.idle: Invite them in: “Want to see how Singapore’s water becomes a lesson in two minutes?”
talk.h1: This is Chora’s real map. Flags are ideas this learner has won; the glowing one has new ideas waiting from Pingu. Ask the visitor to open it.
talk.h2: The Companion suggests linked ideas. The learner decides what joins the map, not the AI.
talk.h3: One AI wrote this question for this learner; a second AI checked it before they saw it. “How was this made?” shows the run.
talk.h4: Same person, now a teacher. The critic AI accepted this draft, but one option could also be right: ask the AI for a new draft, or edit it by hand. The teacher stays in charge.
talk.h4b: Same question, now its picture: fix the diagram, turn it into an illustration, then restyle it, from a pencil sketch to photorealistic.
talk.h5: Let the credits play. Then: Explore more for the curious, Done for the next guest.
talk.hall: Match the exhibit to the person: maps for educators, companions for the young at heart, the dashboard and grading for teachers, the Engine Room for engineers. Show Companions before Grading: releasing a grade also grows the active Companion, so its level-up is best seen in Companions first.
talk.maps: This is Chora’s real map: the lens brings the idea you pick to the centre. The drawer shows its ladder, a practice question and its Companion’s suggestions.
talk.comp: Each Companion is bound to one map. It suggests ideas to march into, quizzes you on the map, and greets your daily dose. Win a hex and watch Pingu grow.
talk.grade: Multiple choice is marked by rules, with no AI. Open answers get an AI score, an AI check and a human review. Here the visitor is the human: adjust a score, then approve.
talk.engine: For engineers: two agent crews, one model gateway, and a governance board that shows red when it should.
talk.crews: Every model call leaves through one gateway. The decision log is hash-chained, so a changed row is detectable.
talk.gov: Say it plainly: this board is a static snapshot from 10 Aug. The computer runs no telemetry engine.
talk.local: Explain how this demo compares with the full platform, starting with the safety screen that is simulated here.
talk.dash: Questions a teacher keeps go into a question bank, and the bank feeds an assessment. In Chora the instructor invites learners; here the visitor takes one straight away. Each assessment mixes multiple choice, with and without a picture, and an open answer with its own picture.
talk.dashTake: Multiple choice is marked by rules on the server the moment they submit, with no AI. An open answer waits for the grading crew and then a person: take it to “Get an answer graded” to grade it live.
talk.safety: For engineers: the release gate is fail-closed. Show 24 Aug: one attack leaked, two members passed, and nothing shipped. The drift proof is a planted test, so say so.

comp.intro: In discover mode, each of your maps has a Companion. It remembers what you find hard, and uses that to choose your daily dose and the ideas to march into next.
comp.bridge: The ideas in step 2 and the question in step 3 came from Pingu, your water map’s Companion. Here you watch the Companions do that work, and more: each one’s weakness analyser reads a marked test paper for weak spots. Win a hex and a Companion grows.
dbx.mcqNote: Marked by rules, not AI: the answer key was written with this question when it was generated, so the same answer always gets the same mark. Only open answers go to the grading crew.
stamp.what: Prepared: made in advance for this demo, by the same AI pipeline you see here. It is what shows without internet, or when a live call runs late. Press a LIVE button to ask the AI now.
live.suggEmpty: Nothing new this time: every idea it found is already on your map or was suggested before.
xr.d4nScene: Q2’s and Q3’s pictures were made by the image model for this demo, and both carry the AI mark.

comp.weakHint: {{name}} reads a test paper its learner sat, marked by a teacher, and proposes the weak spots it finds. You decide which ones it keeps.
comp.weakSaved: Saved. {{name}} keeps {{n}} weak spots, to tailor your daily dose and the ideas to march into.
comp.weakSavedOne: Saved. {{name}} keeps {{n}} weak spot, to tailor your daily dose and the ideas to march into.
comp.weakSavedNone: Saved. {{name}} keeps none of these weak spots, so this paper changes nothing in your daily dose or the ideas to march into.
local.r10c: A text embedding model on Google Cloud, through Chora’s model gateway
local.r10h: A text embedding model, through the same gateway: after “Save my choices” on a marked test, your Companion matches each weak spot you keep to an idea on your map
comp.weakSaveOff: Save is off for now: saving needs Google’s AI online to match each weak spot to your map.
comp.weakNotSaved: Not saved: {{name}} could not finish matching your choices to your map. This paper cannot be saved again in this demo session.
local.r11c: Learners buy mana through Stripe, by Chora’s payments service
local.r11h: Stripe is not connected in this local version: nothing is paid on this computer. Mana goes back to the prepared balance after each demo session
db.manaNote: In this demo, a LIVE press for fresh ideas spends 100 and “Keep and continue” in step 4 spends 20.
xr.weakNoScreen: The paper was not screened: this local edition skips the image safety check, takes only the prepared papers, and reads only the essay live.
kd.sugg.full: No room: an idea holds six at most
comp.paperTap: Tap the paper to see how {{name}} read it
comp.paperHow: The AI reads the whole paper and proposes weak spots without question numbers. Each sits under the question its own words name; one that names no single question is listed apart.
comp.paperNone: No weak spot names this question.
comp.paperApart: Also proposed, not tied to one question
comp.paperEarlier: These weak spots were saved before this demo session, so they are not listed here.

own.title: Your own goal, and a Companion for it
own.line: How it works at home: add your own goal, and a Companion hatches to learn it with you. This is a picture of the full Chora app; the kiosk shows it without taking a payment.
